fact: In winter 2022–23, during La Niña, PM2.5 in north India was up to 30% lower than the 2019–22 winter average.
source: Times of India, ‘Study traces how an El Niño changed the pollution map’; article’s summary of the Atmospheric Pollution Research study.

fact: In winter 2022–23, Mumbai’s average PM2.5 rose by about 45% relative to the 2019–22 winter average.
source: Times of India article on the ENSO pollution study.

fact: In winter 2023–24, during El Niño, Jaipur’s PM2.5 rose by about 50% and Delhi’s rose by over 10% relative to the 2019–22 winter average; the pattern reversed in peninsular India.
source: Times of India article on the ENSO pollution study.

fact: Year-to-year PM2.5 changes ranged from about a 40% decline to a 70% increase relative to the 2019–22 average, despite no major change in emissions or pollution-control policies.
source: Times of India article summarising the Atmospheric Pollution Research study.

fact: In the 2022–23 La Niña winter, stronger winds over north India dispersed emissions from stubble burning and local sources; circulation bypassed Delhi and carried pollutants south toward cities including Mumbai and Thiruvananthapuram.
source: Times of India article citing the Atmospheric Pollution Research study.

fact: In the 2023–24 El Niño winter, winds over northern India were weaker and passed through Delhi and Jaipur rather than carrying pollutants away, favouring pollution build-up.
source: Times of India article citing the Atmospheric Pollution Research study.

fact: Rainfall was more strongly associated with lower PM2.5 in 2022–23. In 2023–24, surface pressure mattered more: high pressure, weak winds and a shallow boundary layer can trap pollutants near the ground.
source: Times of India article on the ENSO pollution study.

fact: Backward air-mass trajectories indicated Jaipur received air from polluted northern regions during the 2023–24 El Niño winter, while Hyderabad received cleaner marine and southern air.
source: Times of India article on the ENSO pollution study.

fact: The article explains that low local or agricultural emissions do not automatically guarantee cleaner air if large-scale circulation is stagnant; stronger winds can disperse pollution even where emissions are high.
source: Times of India article on the ENSO pollution study.

fact: The study’s authors caution that the observed correlations do not prove direct causality, cannot simply be extrapolated to other years, and do not mean El Niño invariably worsens Delhi or north Indian air quality. The comparison covers only two unusual winters.
source: Times of India article reporting the study’s caveats.

fact: A separate IMD/IITM study reported that in northwest India the hot semi-arid zone expanded from about one-quarter of the region in 1951–60 to about one-third in 1991–2020, while the temperate zone shrank from about one-quarter to under one-fifth.
source: Times of India article on the IMD/IITM climate-zone study.

fact: The hot, dry zone has shifted east into Uttar Pradesh, an important farming region; the article says sowing and harvesting timing should be watched closely.
source: Times of India article reporting the IMD/IITM study; the sowing/harvesting point is attributed to lead author Ananya Karmakar.

fact: In peninsular India, the hot semi-arid zone shrank from about 30% of the region to 16%, with much of the area shifting to tropical savannah; the article attributes this pattern to rising rainfall in southern India.
source: Times of India article on the IMD/IITM climate-zone study.

fact: The article reports that Marathwada and west Vidarbha moved into the hot semi-arid zone, while the tropical monsoon zone extended along the Konkan coast, coastal Karnataka and Kerala.
source: Times of India article on the IMD/IITM climate-zone study.

fact: The article describes two related but distinct strands of evidence: a study of PM2.5 patterns across two winters and an IMD/IITM study of climate-zone changes over decades.
source: Synthesis of the two studies as presented in the assigned Times of India article.
